papers.title: View Management with Gaussian Placement and Opacity Regularization for Online 3DGS
papers.abstract: The realistic rendering of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has drawn interest from real-time applications that require maps to be built online. This led to coupling 3DGS with SLAM, providing camera poses and initial Gaussians for the map. However, the map is still optimized with designs inherited from conventional SLAM, which train only on keyframes selected for localization and regularize geometry with uncertain frontend depth. These designs overlook the model complexity of a 3DGS map: with millions of parameters but few views of each region, the map overfits to sparse inputs. Resolving this is challenging, as every view and Gaussian added to the map competes for the same real-time budget. We close this gap from both sides. To add views while keyframes preserve the structure of the map, we progressively admit non-keyframe images as mapping updates complete and allocate the limited updates across different groups of frames according to the supervision each group provides. To control the model complexity of the map, edge-guided initialization places new Gaussians where image detail requires them. To complement the uncertain frontend depth, Self-Referenced Opacity Regularization (SOR) uses accumulated rendering evidence, at no extra rendering cost, to suppress the opacity of Gaussians that persistently contribute in front of a map-derived surface reference. Together, these designs improve both the appearance and the geometry of online maps within the real-time budget.

papers.title: TACTUS: Unifying Surgical Action Understanding in Time and Space
papers.abstract: Advancing surgical automation requires a comprehensive spatio-temporal understanding of how instruments act on tissue throughout an action. Existing surgical benchmarks, however, largely define supervision through task-specific targets, leaving the relationships between action semantics, instrument motion, and tissue interaction incompletely specified. To address this limitation, we introduce TACTUS (Tool, Action, Contact and Trajectory Understanding in Surgery), a new dataset and benchmark that establishes a unified annotation framework for complete surgical actions. The framework jointly specifies tool and action identities, nested action and interaction windows, instrument-specific landmark trajectories, and tissue-region tracks. To construct these annotations at scale, we develop a two-tier pipeline combining human annotation, point tracking, and model-generated spatial prompts. Using this pipeline, we re-annotate 141 videos from five public sources, producing 22,995 action clips spanning 2.9 million frames. The dataset comprises 15,668 Gold clips with human spatial prompts followed by review and re-checking, and 7,327 Silver clips combining human semantic and temporal annotations with model-generated spatial prompts. We further introduce TactusNet, the companion reference network, to benchmark semantic, temporal, and spatial prediction from shared video features. Across TactusNet and 13 published baselines, tool-action accuracy reaches 95.8% with per-head encoder fine-tuning, while the best temporal recall and contact Dice reach 46.6% at temporal IoU 0.7 and 0.351, respectively. Moreover, adding Silver improves the default TactusNet's pair accuracy from 93.8% to 95.5%. Together, these contributions establish a foundation for learning and evaluating the instrument-tissue interactions underlying future surgical automation.

papers.title: Perception Is Enough, at the Right Scale: Scale-Adaptive Token Pruning for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models must process continuous streams of visual observations, and the resulting computational cost limits real-time robotic control. Token pruning reduces this cost, but a fixed semantic scale of perceptual representation can overlook information needed at different stages of manipulation. We show that perceptual semantics can guide effective token selection without relying on internal attention when the selection scale adapts to the scene's evolving semantic structure. Based on this observation, we introduce TauPrune-VLA, a training-free method that controls the scale of the retained perceptual representation through a single perception temperature $\tau$. To adapt this scale as manipulation proceeds, TauPrune-VLA updates $\tau$ online using trends in perceptual semantics, with robot-state changes and action magnitude regulating the adjustment strength. While these semantics evolve over the course of manipulation, they remain relatively stable between consecutive frames. This continuity allows retention indices computed from the current observation to be applied at the next policy invocation, enabling token selection to run asynchronously with inference and reducing pruning overhead. Evaluated across diverse VLA models and simulation benchmarks, TauPrune-VLA achieves up to a $1.86\times$ inference speedup while maintaining near-baseline task success rates. We further validate its effectiveness on two real-world robotic platforms.

papers.title: VLG-Drive: Unifying Vision-Language and Geometric Priors for Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: A driving planner needs both scene semantics, which vision-language models (VLMs) provide, and spatial structure, which geometric foundation models recover from visual history. We present VLG-Drive, which keeps both models frozen and trains only a fusion interface and a planner from trajectory labels. At each camera-grid cell, the interface fuses the paired VLM and geometry features into one joint token through a geometry-anchored residual, and a command-conditioned planner reads these tokens to predict the ego trajectory. VLG-Drive achieves 31.78 EPDMS on NavHard under perturbed initial states, the highest among the compared methods, and 88.27 PDMS on NavTest from cameras alone. Pointwise fusion outperforms independent VLM and geometry streams on both benchmarks. In closed-loop driving on 420 HUGSIM scenarios, VLG-Drive outperforms all compared planners. These results indicate that a lightweight planner trained on fused features of frozen vision-language and geometric foundation models is an effective alternative to adapting either model for planning.

papers.title: DUALingo: A Dual-Hand Instruction-Guided Dataset for Affordance Grounding on 3D Objects
papers.abstract: Affordance grounding localizes where an agent should interact with an object to perform a task. Many everyday manipulation tasks, however, require bimanual affordance, in which two hands assume complementary and cooperative roles to accomplish a shared goal. Existing 3D affordance datasets primarily ground single interaction regions, and manually annotating dual-hand, cooperative contacts does not scale. To address this gap, we introduce DUALingo, a large-scale dataset for task-conditioned, role-aware bimanual 3D affordance grounding on diverse everyday objects. DUALingo represents each task as two cooperative, hand-agnostic roles, each grounded as a heatmap on the object surface. It contains 271K free-form tasks on 71K objects, generated by a fully automated pipeline of open-weight foundation models without human labeling. Expert ratings and a validated LLM judge confirm the quality of the resulting annotations. Trained on DUALingo, existing 3D affordance models learn to ground both cooperative roles from natural-language instructions, with the best-performing model achieving a more than threefold improvement in aIoU over the zero-shot baseline, from 10.3 to 37.8. Robotic manipulation demonstrations illustrate the actionability of the predicted bimanual affordances in performing cooperative tasks. These results position DUALingo as a scalable foundation for learning everyday bimanual affordances. Project page: this https URL

papers.title: Beyond Expert Replay: Cross-Instruction Anchoring for Continual Vision-Language-Action Learning
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models need to continually acquire new manipulation skills while retaining the ability to follow previously learned instructions. Experience replay (ER) can mitigate catastrophic forgetting, but retaining only a small number of historical expert frames per task leaves many old-instruction responses without direct supervision. Under limited replay, we observe a structured failure mode in which an earlier instruction can trigger a subsequently learned, competing goal. To address this gap, we propose Cross-Instruction Anchoring (XIA), which supplements expert replay with instruction-conditioned response preservation. At each task boundary, XIA freezes the previous policy as a teacher and matches its responses to old instructions paired with current observations. This extends supervision beyond stored historical examples without requiring additional expert replay data. Experiments across multiple VLA architectures and three LIBERO suites demonstrate improved success rates and reduced forgetting compared with ER under identical historical expert-data budgets. Additional RoboCasa and real-world experiments further support the effectiveness of XIA.

papers.title: G0.7: Scaling Up a Fast World Action Model with Long Context
papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) adapt pretrained video generators for robot control by jointly predicting future camera frames and actions, transferring physical priors learned from video into manipulation policies. However, generating future frames before every action makes test-time inference too slow for closed-loop control, while most existing policies remain restricted to short observation histories. Building on Fast-WAM, which showed that video prediction shapes policy representations during training so that future frame synthesis can be skipped at deployment, we present G0.7, a generalist world action model scaled along two axes: extending the context window from a single observation to up to five minutes of history, and scaling pretraining to a large-scale corpus of robot teleoperation and human egocentric (ego) video. Across public simulation suites and real-robot deployments, direct action decoding (Fast mode) matches imagine-then-act (IDM) inference from the same checkpoint while running in 60 ms per 16-step action chunk on a single RTX 5090 (7.6x faster than IDM) and supporting pause-free real-time chunking. Performance scales consistently with pretraining data, with human ego video driving the largest gains in out-of-distribution generalization: G0.7 achieves a 70.8 mean score across five simulation benchmark suites, 48% and 54% zero-shot pick-and-place success on Galaxea R1 Pro and R1 Lite, 96.7% in-distribution and 93.3% out-of-distribution success on video-conditioned in-context learning tasks, and 86.9% mean task progress across seven real-world post-training tasks including multi-minute box folding, drink preparation, and product bagging. papers.title: LeanWAM: Learning Latent World Action Models from Frozen Video Models
papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) typically adapt large pretrained video generators to jointly predict future observations and robot actions, incurring substantial training and deployment costs. However, it remains unclear which future representations a policy actually needs and how compactly they can be represented. Our probing study shows that complementary future representations can be compressed into a few tokens while retaining most of their action-decoding performance. Motivated by this finding, we introduce LeanWAM, a latent WAM that transfers video priors from a frozen video generator to a lightweight policy via two-stage training. In the first stage, a Future Extractor compresses observed transitions into 32 predictive tokens. These tokens condition the frozen generator and are jointly shaped by action, RGB, semantic, and geometric supervision, while a compact readout of the generator's hidden states supplies complementary world tokens. The second stage distills both representations into the policy, which learns to predict them from current observations while generating actions. With 1.4B parameters and no large-scale embodied pretraining, LeanWAM outperforms strong vision-language-action (VLA) and WAM baselines on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin~2.0. It predicts an action chunk in 25.1\,ms on an A100 GPU, 12.3--41.5$\times$ faster than representative WAMs. These results demonstrate that compact predictive supervision can transfer video priors to robust and efficient control.

papers.title: The cyborg fly: reflexes survive engineered actuators, coordination needs stand-ins
papers.abstract: Two wiring diagrams now cover the whole central nervous system of an adult fruit fly: one female, one male. Can such a diagram, run as a network of spiking neurons, drive a body? And if we swap the body's muscles for engineered actuators, what survives? We ran both connectomes, BANC and MaleCNS, as leaky integrate-and-fire networks of about 160,000 neurons each, and closed the loop through simulated sensors, actuators and bodies for walking and flight. The actuators are port-Hamiltonian, so energy is audited at every step, and swapping one for another changes only a configuration file. Null networks shuffled at five levels, from the whole nervous system to synapse counts, test whether a result depends on the wiring. The wiring produced specific functions: sugar on the labellum drove the proboscis motor neuron, leg joints resisted imposed movement, leg circuits oscillated, a looming disc drove a take-off signal on its side (in MaleCNS), and descending neurons throttled and steered flight. The resistance reflex survived 20 of 20 actuator settings in MaleCNS and 19 of 20 in BANC, including a Hill-type muscle pair and a geared DC motor; the actuator set walking speed and energy cost instead. Coordinated six-leg walking, flight stability and the correction of perturbations did not emerge. Each needed a labelled engineered stand-in, which the connectome could command. Such stand-ins can also manufacture an apparent dependence on wiring: in a rebuild of a published closed loop, odour navigation came from a hand-written rule, and the network entered only through one valence number. The two animals differed on some functions, and the differences traced to wiring, such as a haltere drive of the flight power muscles found only in MaleCNS. A whole-CNS connectome, embodied, gives reflexes, rhythms and command signals, but not the coordination that turns them into behaviour.

papers.title: One Phase Is Enough: Sim-to-Real Transfer with Direct Visual Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Sim-to-real reinforcement learning (RL) has enabled impressive robotic behaviors, yet deploying policies directly from vision remains challenging. A common approach first trains a teacher policy with RL using privileged state observations, then distills its behavior into a vision-based student via imitation. However, the resulting student can substantially underperform its teacher. Directly training visual policies with RL offers a promising alternative, but learning task-relevant visual representations from scratch can be sample-inefficient, making one-phase visual RL intractable. We propose DRIFT, a simple recipe for efficient one-phase visual RL using image observations available at test time. Our key insight is to use frozen, pretrained foundation vision encoders, allowing RL to focus on learning control from existing visual representations. Freezing the encoder avoids costly backpropagation through the vision backbone, while its pretrained representations enable real-world transfer from fast, rasterized simulation rendering. Under matched architectures, observations, and compute budgets, DRIFT outperforms two-phase distillation and achieves a 58.8% relative improvement in average real-world success rate across three manipulation tasks. Controlled simulation evaluations demonstrate that DRIFT's relative advantage grows from roughly 9% in-distribution to over 61% under out-of-distribution shifts, suggesting that stronger generalization contributes to superior real-world transfer. papers.title: Near-Zero Forgetting Is Not Enough: Out-of-Distribution Robustness in Continual Learning of Pretrained VLAs
papers.abstract: Recent work shows that pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models exhibit near-zero forgetting in specific continual learning settings with experience replay. However, robustness to domain shift of learned tasks remains unexplored. In this work, we study the robustness of Pi0 fine-tuned with experience replay under out-of-distribution (OOD) data using the LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus benchmarks. While the in-domain (ID) setup achieves near-zero catastrophic forgetting, OOD performance on previous tasks quickly collapses. Specifically, we show that during the continual learning process, the OOD capabilities of the model degrade, following a shared representational pattern across domain shifts, which is also visible behaviorally in the two simpler suites. Representational analysis shows that drift concentrates in the multimodal and action features. Linear probes indicate that OOD features still retain task-relevant information, but appear unreadable, consistent with representation misalignment. These findings suggest that even when ID stability remains intact, severe OOD forgetting can still occur, accompanied by representational drift during continual learning.

executive_summary: Multiple systems advance dexterous, contact-rich manipulation: a five-finger tendon-driven Soft-Rigid Hybrid Hand with 12 active DoF achieves 28/33 (84.8%) human-range grasp postures and up to 1432 deg/s joint extension in teleoperated soft and delicate manipulation tasks; ViTacLab couples a tri-modal visuo-tactile simulator, benchmark, and policy, reaching 2,482.9 tactile-pipeline FPS with 256 environments and cutting normal/tangential force RMSE from 2.31→0.42 N and 1.85→0.53 N, though success on purely tactile-dominant tasks remains low; FabricBench provides six bimanual fabric tasks with 10,000 assets and a Newton-based simulator whose solver succeeds in 45/45 grasp–hold–release trials where baselines fail, yet best learned policies still struggle on long-horizon and highly deformed T-shirt configurations; HiMoDex pretrains a hierarchical multimodal (vision, tactile, force-torque, audio) representation then a shared world-action transformer, achieving 78.7% average success ( +32.0 points over the strongest baseline) on five real bimanual dexterous tasks; Ego2Real leverages egocentric video plus tactile-glove data for bimanual skill transfer, using tactile-guided reconstruction and contact-informed RL, and reports higher manipulation success when tactile supervision is used in both stages than in ablated variants.

New policy architectures broaden generality across embodiments and arms while improving dynamic control: OmniAct conditions on each robot’s kinematic graph and uses flow matching over joint deltas, trained on 1M simulated embodiments to achieve 63.0% success on 2,000 held-out embodiment–scene episodes (vs. 17.8% for π₀.₅ and 57.9% for the best baseline), 64.7% success on GPT-6 Astra task families (vs. 41.1%), and nearly 2× the success of MolmoAct2 on a previously unseen real robot; Duo treats each arm as an action token within a shared head with cross-arm attention, yielding RoboTwin 2.0 gains of 12.55 and 9.02 percentage points for FLOWER (0.89B) and π₀.₅ (3.62B), and enabling compact FLOWER-Duo to attain top randomized-generalization, precision, and memory on RoboDojo and better real-world success and speed than π₀.₅; Co-DRIS + SuperMimic co-designs perception and control for reactive catching with a physics-informed world-frame model, dual-stream causal GRU belief encoder, and phase-aware variable-impedance control, achieving 89.6 ± 0.4% success on standard benchmarks (70.5% at 4σ noise) and 66.6 ± 0.5% across 10 stress scenarios, with large gains over DRIS and improved catching and reduced impact forces in transfer tasks.

World(-action) modeling methods target more efficient and interpretable control: DexWAC jointly trains an action-conditioned world model, actor, and bootstrapped critic using an image-editing backbone that predicts endpoint visual latents, proprioception, reward, and continuation per action chunk, then improves the actor via PPO or critic-guided best-of-N over imagined rollouts, achieving 75% average success on two real dexterous tasks vs. 45% for π₀.₅ and reporting faster, more accurate dynamics than video-based baselines; iWAM conditions a policy on intermediate features from a single evaluation of a pretrained video model by inverting futures into latent noise with flow matching and learning a bidirectional flow map, matching the generalization of full video-prediction WAMs while cutting inference cost for real-time control; SimPWM represents scenes with an explicit 3D robot model and point-based objects evolved by a rule-based simulator and rendered by a video model, improving robot IoU to 0.75–0.78 on unseen DROID setups (vs. ≤0.69 end-to-end) and reducing missed pick-ups from 54% to 38% when adding simulated objects, while analyses show that explicit simulated state remains reliable even when rendered video disagrees; PILOT augments World Action Models with a Representational Deduction mechanism that introduces motion chain-of-thought via explicit state-transition tokens, which the authors report improves success and generalization on complex manipulation, enhances physical interpretability, and enables more data-efficient real-robot adaptation under reduced demonstrations.

Several works address temporal dynamics, latency, and tactile/force inference in perception–action loops: FoveaWAM is a 4D world-action model that allocates precision to the target object’s SE(3) trajectory and sparse 3D flow for surroundings while reusing the current frame for static context, achieving 15.1 ms action latency on a single RTX 5090 (≈10× faster than video-based WAMs) and 82.1% success on OnTimeBench (20.8 points above the strongest baseline) plus leading results on DOMINO and real robots; VidForce learns shared force-level and temporal prototypes from limited instrumented data to jointly infer interaction trajectories and force profiles from third-person RGB, reaching 6.6 cm ATE, peak-force MAE/RMSE of 4.81/5.92 N, and force-profile RMSE of 5.52 N on held-out Hoi! interactions, and enabling Spot to manipulate articulated objects using inferred trajectories and forces.

Training recipes, datasets, and benchmarks expose gaps and improve data efficiency: DRIFT trains sim-to-real visual RL policies in a single phase by freezing foundation vision encoders and learning only the control layer, yielding a 58.8% relative gain in average real-world success over matched two-phase distillation methods and larger simulated advantages under out-of-distribution shifts (>61% relative) than in-distribution (~9%); β-Data collects adversarial teleoperation where one human perturbs the environment while another completes the task and relabels segments with local language outcomes, and midtraining on this dataset with recent-action conditioning produces policies with better data scaling, zero-shot generalization, extended-horizon benefits, and more sample-efficient online finetuning than standard demonstrations across simulated and three real-robot platforms; RoboClock defines 60 manipulation tasks with explicit temporal constraints and latency-aligned evaluation, and finds that the best trained VLA attains only 8.3% temporal success even on Easy tasks, indicating pronounced deficits in temporal reasoning and transfer.

Additional contributions span multi-agent optimization, adaptation, and higher-level reasoning and assistance: DS-TO is a fully decentralized distributed sampling-based trajectory optimizer that has each agent sample only in its own control space while communicating with neighbors, and experiments on 2D/3D tasks with up to 1024 agents report improved exploration, constraint satisfaction, and scalability over derivative-based and sampling baselines; R2R’s deployment-localization plus Human-Anchored RL adapts released autonomous-driving planners and perception to new vehicles and sensors, raising a diffusion planner’s closed-loop success from 82.2% to 95.2% and boosting a released multi-camera detector’s mAP from 0.041 to 0.420 on a five-camera rig without target labels; Ada-BFM adds lightweight adapters to Behavior Foundation Models for humanoid scene interaction, enabling shared-domain models that handle diverse terrains and object contacts in sim and real while accelerating learning and largely preserving prior skills; an offline RL method learns a help-seeking policy that tailors human-intervention alerts to past helpfulness and autonomous progress, improving exploration and reducing unnecessary alerts in simulation and enhancing novice support without harming expert performance in a physical user study; Embodied Neuro-Symbolic AI is proposed as a deployment-oriented paradigm that combines learned perception and control with explicit background knowledge and formal constraints to enable robots that can reason about environments, adapt to new tasks, and provide auditable compliance.

institution_matches.title: Design, Control, and Teleoperation of a Dexterous Robotic Hand with Soft-Rigid Hybrid Fingers
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes a five-fingered tendon-driven Soft-Rigid Hybrid Hand with 12 active DoF, combining structural compliance with a rigid skeleton to enable linear control for soft grasping and teleoperated manipulation. In evaluation of grasp postures within the human range, the proposed hand successfully achieves 28 of 33 (84.8%) grasp postures and demonstrates high-bandwidth motion, reaching up to 1432 deg/s extension speed compared to about 700 deg/s for the equivalent human joint. Teleoperation experiments on various grasping and non-rigid manipulation tasks (e.g., picking up thin deformable objects and interacting with soft or delicate targets) indicate that the hand’s mechanical design and control strategy are effective for compliant, dexterous manipulation.

institution_matches.title: OmniAct: One Policy, One Million Embodiments
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces OmniAct, a cross-embodiment manipulation policy that conditions directly on each robot’s kinematic graph (joint positions, motion axes, and connectivity to vision) and uses flow matching to predict relative joint motions for robots with diverse degrees of freedom and configurations. Trained on procedurally generated trajectories for one million simulated robot embodiments across diverse manipulation tasks, OmniAct achieves 63.0% success on 2,000 embodiment-scene-held-out evaluation episodes, outperforming pi 0.5 (17.8%) and the strongest baseline (57.9%). On the task families used to evaluate GPT-6 Astra, OmniAct reaches 64.7% success versus 41.1% for GPT-6 Astra, and on a previously unseen real-world robot it attains nearly twice the success rate of the next best method (MolmoAct2), while exhibiting distinct morphology-dependent manipulation strategies.

institution_matches.title: Sampling at Scale: Distributed Multi-Agent Trajectory Optimization
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes DS-TO (Distributed Sampling-based Trajectory Optimization), a distributed architecture that splits multi-agent trajectory optimization so each agent samples only in its own control space, independent of neighborhood size, while still incorporating constraint-induced non-convexity and neighbors’ decisions. DS-TO is fully decentralized, relying only on neighborhood communication with parallel local updates, and includes efficient variants such as parallel Jacobi updates within each subproblem and single-step constraint linearization to reduce computation. Experiments on 2D and 3D multi-agent tasks with up to 1024 agents show that DS-TO improves exploration and constraint satisfaction compared to state-of-the-art derivative-based distributed optimization methods, and scales better than existing distributed sampling approaches.

institution_matches.title: Duo: Towards Spatiotemporal Action Coordination in Bimanual Policies
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces Duo, a bimanual manipulation policy architecture that represents each arm as a separate action token per timestep within a shared action head, enabling cross-arm attention during flow matching to model both spatial and temporal dependencies. On the RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark, Duo improves overall success for all four evaluated base policies (0.45B–3.62B parameters), yielding gains of 12.55 and 9.02 percentage points for FLOWER (0.89B) and π₀.₅ (3.62B), respectively. Despite its compact size, FLOWER-Duo attains the best randomized-generalization, precision, and memory scores on RoboDojo, and in real-world tasks it outperforms π₀.₅ in both success rate and execution speed; ablations indicate that cross-arm attention and arm-wise interaction are key to the accuracy-compute trade-off.

institution_matches.title: ViTacLab: Physically Consistent Visuo-Tactile Simulation, Benchmarking, and Representation Learning for Robotic Manipulation
institution_matches.overview: The paper presents ViTacLab, consisting of ViTacSim (a tri-modal visuo-tactile simulator), ViTacBench (a benchmark suite), and ViTacPolicy (a visuo-tactile policy architecture) to support physically consistent visuo-tactile simulation and learning for contact-rich robotic manipulation across grippers, dexterous hands, and bimanual systems. ViTacSim combines a global sparse contact-force lattice, a local dense force array, and tactile images anchored to PhysX contact outputs, and uses local stiffness alignment, decoupled slip–stick reconstruction, and joint projection to correct normal/tangential inconsistencies while maintaining GPU-parallel throughput of 2,482.9 tactile-pipeline FPS with 256 parallel environments. In controlled Hertzian indentation and real-sensor sliding tests, ViTacSim reduces normal and tangential force RMSE from 2.31 N to 0.42 N and from 1.85 N to 0.53 N, respectively; simulation and real-world experiments show performance gains on several contact-rich tasks, though absolute success remains low on tactile-dominant tasks, underscoring the difficulty of purely tactile control.

institution_matches.title: DexWAC: A Unified World-Actor-Critic Model for Dexterous Robot Manipulation
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes DexWAC, a unified world-actor-critic model that jointly learns an action-conditioned world model, an actor, and a bootstrapped critic in a single pretraining stage, using visual prediction for control-relevant features and value prediction for task-relevant representations. Built on an image-editing backbone, DexWAC predicts for each action chunk the endpoint visual latent, proprioception, reward, and continuation, enabling efficient imagined transitions without generating intermediate frames, and subsequently improves the actor via PPO on imagined rollouts or critic-guided best-of-N selection after world-model and critic adaptation on real rollouts. In simulation and on two real-world dexterous manipulation tasks, DexWAC outperforms large-scale pretrained VLA and WAM baselines, achieving 75% average real-world success compared to 45% for π₀.₅, with a world model that is both more accurate and faster than video-based baselines; ablations support the benefit of jointly learning dynamics and value.

institution_matches.title: VidForce: Predicting Force-Aware Articulation by Observing Humans
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces VidForce, a method that estimates both an interaction trajectory and a force profile from third-person RGB videos of human interactions, optionally using 2D contact clicks and text object–action prompts, by leveraging learned physical prototypes from limited instrumented force measurements. VidForce uses shared force-level and temporal-profile prototypes as priors across interactions of similar effort, refines them with geometric and vision-language features, and jointly predicts trajectories and forces via a conditional flow model; a separate torque model shows extensibility to other physical quantities. On held-out interactions from the Hoi! dataset, VidForce achieves 6.6 cm ATE, peak-force MAE/RMSE of 4.81 N/5.92 N, and force-profile RMSE of 5.52 N; it produces consistent motion and force estimates on real-world videos and enables Spot robot manipulation of articulated objects using trajectories and force profiles inferred from human demonstrations.

institution_matches.title: Exploratory Midtraining for Robot Policies
institution_matches.institution: Carnegie Mellon University; University of Washington
institution_matches.overview: The paper studies midtraining for robot policies and introduces β-Data, a dataset collected via adversarial teleoperation in which a human adversary reversibly perturbs the environment while another operator continues toward task completion, producing trajectories that richly cover low-level behaviors without resets. Trajectory segments in β-Data are relabeled with local natural-language outcomes, and a pretrained policy is finetuned on this data while being conditioned on recent action history, yielding policies that exhibit more sustained use of diverse low-level behaviors. Across simulated manipulation tasks and three real-robot platforms, midtraining with β-Data leads to more favorable data scaling, better zero-shot generalization, improved benefits from extended rollout time, and more sample-efficient online finetuning (fewer rollouts and higher eventual success) compared to training on standard demonstration data.

institution_matches.title: iWAM: Efficient Action Prediction from World Models without Explicit Future Prediction
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes iWAM, an efficient world-action-model variant that conditions a policy on intermediate features from a single evaluation of a pretrained video model, avoiding explicit high-resolution future prediction while retaining the benefits of world models for action prediction. iWAM inverts each training future frame into a latent noise vector using flow-matching dynamics and learns a bidirectional flow map that amortizes future-generation computation so that a single velocity evaluation at inference (from a sampled prior latent) yields informative conditioning features for the policy. Across simulated benchmarks and real-robot experiments, iWAM matches the generalization benefits of full video-prediction WAMs while substantially reducing inference cost for real-time control.

institution_matches.title: Simulator-as-Proxy World Model for Robot Manipulation
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces SimPWM (Simulator-as-Proxy World Model), which represents a scene from the first frame using a calibrated 3D robot model and point-based object representations, applies a parameter-free rule-based simulator to evolve their state under actions, and uses a video model to render realistic future frames while exposing the explicit simulated state. On DROID episodes from unseen setups, SimPWM shows that video models strongly follow the simulated robot arm proxy (robot IoU 0.75–0.78, exceeding at most 0.69 for end-to-end models), and that adding simulated objects primarily affects predicted object state, reducing missed pick-ups from 54% to 38% relative to a robot-only proxy. By freezing simulated objects while replaying recorded arm motions, the study reveals that some video models (e.g., MiniMax-H3) faithfully track the simulated object state (rigid objects’ lift rate drops from 42% to 10%), whereas others (e.g., LTX-2.3) often infer grasps from arm motion alone (lift rate only drops from 57% to 49%), and that for all base models the explicit simulated state reliably encodes what the simulator did even when rendered video disagrees under perturbed actions.

institution_matches.title: One Phase Is Enough: Sim-to-Real Transfer with Direct Visual Reinforcement Learning
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes DRIFT, a one-phase sim-to-real visual reinforcement learning recipe that trains control policies directly on image observations by freezing pretrained foundation vision encoders so RL only learns the control layer. In real-world robotic manipulation across three tasks, DRIFT outperforms two-phase distillation methods under matched architectures, observations, and compute, achieving a 58.8% relative improvement in average real-world success rate. Simulation studies show DRIFT’s relative advantage grows from roughly 9% on in-distribution conditions to over 61% under out-of-distribution shifts, indicating improved generalization that supports superior sim-to-real transfer.

institution_matches.title: Roboclock: A Unified Benchmark for Time-Aware Robotic Intelligence
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces RoboClock, a unified time-aware robotic manipulation benchmark with 60 tasks across five domains, structured around three temporal constraint types: Temporal Window, Event-Reactive, and Throughput, and evaluated with a Latency-Aligned protocol and time-sensitive metrics. Across more than 30 evaluated methods, the best-performing trained vision-language-action (VLA) approach achieves only 8.3% temporal success even on Easy-level tasks under RoboClock, revealing substantial deficits in temporal reasoning, generalization, and transfer in current robotic systems.

institution_matches.title: Embodied Neuro-symbolic AI: Making Robot Behavior Auditable, Safe, and Scalable
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes Embodied Neuro-Symbolic (NeSy) AI, a deployment-oriented paradigm that integrates learned perception, planning, and control with explicit machine-readable background knowledge and formal constraints for robotic systems. By combining knowledge-guided perception, constraint-aware symbolic planning, and hybrid learning, Embodied NeSy AI is presented as enabling robots to reason about environments, adapt to new tasks, and provide auditable, machine-checkable compliance with safety and operational requirements.

topic_matches.title: Hi3R-VLA: Grounding Semantics and Actions in 3D
topic_matches.institution: CNRS; INRIA; PSL Research University; École normale supérieure
topic_matches.overview: The paper introduces Hi3R-VLA, a 3D vision-language-action policy that grounds visual, linguistic, and action modalities in explicit 3D geometry by fusing spatially aligned visual features and language into point cloud representations and anchoring low-level control commands in the same 3D frame with 3D-RoPE-enhanced action-to-point attention. Hi3R-VLA, with fewer than 250M trainable parameters, achieves state-of-the-art performance on RoboCasa, RLBench, RoboTwin2, DexJoCo, and DexSuite across diverse robotic manipulation tasks and embodiments, and demonstrates effectiveness in real-robot evaluations.

topic_matches.title: FabricBench: A Standardized Policy Benchmark for Bimanual Fabric Manipulation with a Contact-Driven Deformable Simulator
topic_matches.institution: Horizon Robotics; Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Style3D Research
topic_matches.overview: The paper presents FabricBench, a standardized benchmark for bimanual fabric manipulation featuring six tasks (including garments, silk, and bags), 10,000 simulation-ready assets, and controlled configuration and appearance generalization tests, built on an open-source Newton-based deformable simulator with stable contact-driven bimanual interactions. In a controlled grasp–hold–release evaluation, the proposed solver succeeds in all 45 trials while tested baseline configurations achieve no successes, indicating improved modeling of cloth–rigid and multi-body contact dynamics. Across six evaluated policies, including VLA and world-action models, the best policy attains 77% average success but remains below 36% on long-horizon T-shirt folding and drops to 6–14% success under highly deformed initial T-shirt configurations, highlighting configuration generalization as a key open challenge; zero-shot real-robot deployment of π_{0.5} preserves task difficulty ordering with Spearman ρ=0.94.

topic_matches.title: FoveaWAM: Role-Aware 4D World-Action Modeling for Dynamic Manipulation
topic_matches.institution: Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence; Beijing Zhongguancun Academy; Peking University
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes FoveaWAM, a 4D world-action model for dynamic manipulation that allocates prediction precision by role: modeling the target object as a metric SE(3) trajectory, the surroundings as sparse 3D flow, and relying on the current frame for static context to enable fast, targeted forecasting. FoveaWAM achieves a 15.1 ms action latency on a single RTX 5090, about 10× faster than video-based world-action baselines, thereby reducing scene evolution during inference. On the OnTimeBench dynamic manipulation benchmark with latency-aware evaluation, FoveaWAM attains 82.1% success, outperforming the strongest baseline by 20.8 percentage points, and also leads on DOMINO and real-robot tasks.

topic_matches.title: Many Senses, One World: Learning Hierarchical Multimodal World Representations for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation
topic_matches.institution: National Key Laboratory of Human-Machine Hybrid Augmented Intelligence; Xi'an Jiaotong University
topic_matches.overview: The paper introduces HiMoDex, a two-stage framework for bimanual dexterous manipulation that first pretrains a hierarchical multimodal representation network on 1.19M synchronized timesteps to fuse vision, tactile, force-torque, and audio into world-state embeddings, then freezes this network and trains a shared world-action transformer for action generation and action-conditioned future-state prediction. On five real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks, HiMoDex achieves an average success rate of 78.7%, representing an absolute improvement of 32.0 percentage points over the strongest evaluated baseline. Ablation and failure analyses indicate that hierarchical representation learning and the two-stage training procedure are key contributors to the observed performance gains across tasks.

topic_matches.title: Beyond the Benchmark: Localizing Released Autonomous Driving Models to Real Vehicles
topic_matches.institution: Toyota North America R&D; University of North Texas
topic_matches.overview: The paper studies the deployment gap between released autonomous-driving models and new real-vehicle platforms and introduces Released-to-Real (R2R), a deployment-localization methodology that identifies components coupled to source-system assumptions and corrects only those while preserving the rest of the released model. For data and behavior adaptation, the authors propose Human-Anchored Reinforcement Learning (HA-RL), which addresses mismatch between trajectory-level planning and receding-horizon execution by correcting ego-state handling using recorded target driving, avoiding costly closed-loop RL rollouts; for sensor adaptation, R2R adjusts spatial and temporal representations with frozen perception weights and no target annotations or retraining. Applied to a released diffusion-based planner, HA-RL improves closed-loop success rate from 82.2% to 95.2%, while sensor adaptation across multiple released detectors and three real sensor rigs increases vehicle mAP of a released multi-camera detector from 0.041 to 0.420 on a five-camera target rig.

topic_matches.title: Co-DRIS: Physics-Informed Predictive Belief and Variable-Impedance Learning for Reactive Catching under Coupled Uncertainty
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes Co-DRIS + SuperMimic, a perception–action co-design framework for reactive catching under coupled uncertainties, combining a physics-informed inertial world-frame model with ballistic kinematics and zero-initialized contact residuals, an action-conditioned dual-stream causal GRU belief encoder, and phase-aware variable-impedance soft-catching control for a 7-DoF Franka Research 3 arm. Under unbiased three-seed tail evaluation on unseen throws (15,360 throws per scenario), the method achieves 89.6 ± 0.4% success on standard benchmarks (including an increase to 70.5% at 4-sigma noise) and 66.6 ± 0.5% across 10 coupled/dropout stress scenarios, improving performance by 39.0 percentage points over DRIS and by 30.4 percentage points under 50% observation dropout. Additional experiments validate impedance decoupling, causal contact triggering under +0.65 s flight-time shifts, and cross-task transfer, improving success from 87.5% to 100.0% on steel-plate ping-pong bouncing and achieving +8.4% catching success under 4× noise on FR3+Hand with 6–13% lower peak impact forces.

topic_matches.title: Ada-BFM: Adapting Behavior Foundation Models for Humanoid Scene Interaction
topic_matches.institution: Fudan University; Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory; Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Southeast University; The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Zhejiang University
topic_matches.overview: The paper introduces Ada-BFM, a post-training framework that augments pretrained Behavior Foundation Models with lightweight adapters to enable humanoid scene interaction, allowing scene-dependent geometric constraints and contact dynamics to be handled while leveraging existing whole-body control capabilities. Ada-BFM yields a shared model per interaction domain rather than per task, supporting diverse terrain and object interaction behaviors in simulation and real-world settings, and is reported to accelerate learning compared with training controllers from scratch while largely preserving pretrained behavioral competence.

topic_matches.title: Learning When a Robot Should Ask For Help: Adaptive Intervention Requests in Human-Robot Teaming
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes an offline reinforcement learning algorithm that learns a help-seeking policy for robots, enabling adaptive human intervention requests based on past intervention helpfulness and autonomous progress during human-robot teaming. In simulation across different task environments and user expertise levels, the learned alert policy selectively requests human help, improving exploration efficiency and reducing unnecessary alerts compared to non-adaptive alert strategies. In a physical user study, the learned policy enhances support for novice users without degrading expert user performance in real-time human-robot teaming missions.

topic_matches.title: Ego2Real: Learning Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation from Egocentric Visuo-Tactile Demonstrations
topic_matches.institution: AGILINK; The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology; Zhejiang University
topic_matches.overview: The paper introduces Ego2Real, a framework that uses egocentric visual demonstrations and tactile glove data to transfer bimanual dexterous manipulation skills to anthropomorphic robotic hands. Ego2Real employs tactile-guided hand-object interaction reconstruction to refine human hand poses and contact geometry, and contact-informed reinforcement learning to convert human contact patterns into robot contact rewards during policy training. Experiments on bimanual dexterous manipulation show that incorporating tactile supervision in both reconstruction and policy learning stages increases manipulation success rates relative to variants without such tactile supervision.
claims: The paper introduces Ego2Real, a framework that uses egocentric visual demonstrations and tactile glove data to transfer bimanual dexterous manipulation skills to anthropomorphic robotic hands.

Ego2Real employs tactile-guided hand-object interaction reconstruction to refine human hand poses and contact geometry, and contact-informed reinforcement learning to convert human contact patterns into robot contact rewards during policy training.

topic_matches.title: Motion Chain of Thought: Disentangling Motion Semantics from Visual Appearance for Robotic Manipulation
topic_matches.institution: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology; Joy Future Academy, JD; Nanjing University; The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen; Tsinghua University
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes PILOT (Physical Inference for Latent Optimized Trajectories), which introduces a Representational Deduction mechanism to integrate motion chain-of-thought guidance, encouraging the action branch of World Action Models to explicitly model potential state transition tokens that guide fine-grained motion trajectories. By disentangling high-level motion semantics from low-level trajectory details, the proposed RD mechanism improves success rates and generalization of World Action Models on complex robotic manipulation tasks while enhancing the physical interpretability of the learned models. The additional state-transition supervision signals provided by RD alleviate sparse supervision in action generation, enabling more data-efficient adaptation to real robots with reduced demonstration sets.
